1:
The saying about wine is read as a personification. Keil and Delitzsch render the second clause mead is boisterous rather than strong drink is raging, and note that the article, which the personification requires, stands with the first word only and serves for both; they also correct a claim that it is not original here. The effects, they say, are attributed to the liquors as their own property—wine mocks because the intoxicated readily scoff at what is holy, mead is boisterous because the inebriated break through the limits of propriety—and the man who staggers under it is unwise in being no longer master of himself. Matthew Henry puts it as a sequence: it smiles upon him at first, at the last it bites, and afterwards rages in his conscience; when the wine is in the wit is out, and the man mocks like a fool or rages like a madman according to his temper. Drunkenness pretends to be sociable, he adds, and unfits men for society. Adam Clarke compresses it—it deceives by its fragrance, intoxicates by its strength, and renders the intoxicated ridiculous—the second word covering any strong fermented liquor, of vine, date or palm. John Gill observes that it sets a man scoffing not only at his companions but at religion itself, and Henry adds that the sin does not merely find a man foolish but keeps him so, since it infatuates and takes away the heart.

On the king the readings split by temper. Henry distinguishes two kinds of rule: princes who govern by wisdom and love rule as God does and bear his image, while those who govern by terror alone rule like a forest lion, by brutal power. Charles Ellicott is narrower, taking the dread the king casts as a warning of approaching danger and glossing the second clause as an offence against one’s own life. Gill lifts it to the King of kings, terrible to the drunkards just described, and Adam Clarke notes only that an earlier proverb says almost the same.

The word for meddling divides them, and so does the sluggard’s excuse. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both prefer showing his teeth to meddling, the latter adding that the emphasis falls not on every fool but on the man who is always one and finds positive pleasure in the quarrel; Ellicott thinks he bares them because he supposes his dignity at stake. John Wesley keeps the received sense, a man always ready to begin strife and obstinate in continuing it. They also weigh whether the first clause means to remain far from strife or to desist from it—the choice turns on the vowel pointing, and another scholar prefers the second—but settle on remaining quietly seated, held back from activity of the kind. Henry and Gill agree the honour lies in withdrawing an action or dropping a controversy, and Gill presses the harder case, that even a man in the right does honourably to drop a dispute that will issue in no good and turns only on words. On the ploughing Keil and Delitzsch stand alone. Many interpreters explain the phrase as by reason of the cold, but they argue the word is no synonym for cold: it means the gathering, and since ploughing and sowing there followed the fruit harvest from October to December, the harvest opened the agricultural year—so the sense is temporal, not causal, and the sluggard fails to plough at the beginning of harvest. Clarke keeps the cold but qualifies it: severe weather is seldom seen there, only occasional cold days with wind, rain and sleet, so the excuse is a pretence under which the season is let slip. Henry says as much in his own way, that ploughing time falls not in the depth of winter but in the borders of it, and adds that though it may be charity to relieve sluggards, a man may in justice decline.
5:
The deep water is drawn out for two different reasons. Keil and Delitzsch read the saying adversarially. Still waters are deep, and what a man has secretly planned he conceals, craftily misleading those who try to get at it; the man of understanding, who sees through men and things, penetrates to the bottom of that water and draws the purpose out. He does not deceive himself about people, estimating conduct by its last underlying motive, and meets a design that would harm him while it is still being realised. Matthew Henry allows that use—some by sly insinuations and foreign-seeming questions will get out of a man what he has done and intends, so anyone keeping counsel must stand on his guard—but the opposite case interests him more. Some are excellently able to advise, having a faculty of cleaving a hair and hitting the joint of a difficulty, yet are modest and not communicative: there is a great deal in them, and it is loth to come out. A man of understanding will draw it out as wine from a vessel, and we lose the benefit of wise men’s conversation, Henry adds, for want of the art of being inquisitive. Adam Clarke agrees that the deepest minds rarely join a discourse unsolicited, and calls the metaphor expressive. Charles Ellicott supplies the machinery, a windlass and bucket; John Wesley glosses the counsel as designs of something of moment, secret and hard to discover; John Gill divides the case between wicked men who seek sleep to hide their counsel and studious men who have gathered much and are slow of speech.

The next verse Keil and Delitzsch rewrite entirely. Against the received sense, which they attribute to a string of commentators, they deny that the first line means most men proclaim their own goodness, rendering it, almost every one meets a man who is gracious to him; a further proposal, many a man one names his dear friend, they reject as stylistically impossible. Their contrast is thus not boasting against fidelity but abundance against rarity: patrons who make promises and awaken expectations, then leave in the lurch the man who depended on them, are many; a man who stands the test is hard to find. The others keep the boast. Henry says it is easy to find men who call themselves men of mercy and sound a trumpet over what little goodness they have, and hard to find those who do more than they speak of—such a one is like a black swan. Gill hears the same trumpet and notes the word may be rendered his kindness to the poor. Ellicott puts the point in the gap between intention and performance: full of benevolent intentions, but a faithful man who carries them out, who can find? Clarke gives an old English rendering.

On the just man Keil and Delitzsch spend their space on grammar. They refuse to take the first line as a separate clause with the righteous man as subject or predicate, since so read it holds out no promise and does not answer the second line; and they reject the familiar rendering, the just man walking in his integrity, because putting the adjective first is against Hebrew usage. Their solution takes the word as an accusative of manner: he who in his innocence walks as one upright. Henry, uninterested in grammar, divides the blessing. The man does well for himself, having a rule he governs himself by with an even steady hand, and a good conscience whose comfort is his rejoicing—he is spared the uneasiness in contriving what to do and reflecting on what he has done that those who walk in deceit are liable to. And he does well for his family, since God has mercy in store for the seed of the faithful. Gill grounds the righteousness elsewhere, in a man made righteous by the obedience of Christ.
8:
The king on the seat of judgment is praised for being there himself. Matthew Henry contrasts two ways of occupying a throne: not as a throne of honour, to take one’s ease and make men keep their distance, but as a throne of judgment, redressing the injured and taking cognizance of affairs himself instead of devolving the trouble on others. Adam Clarke points to a court in his own country where the sovereign is always supposed to be sitting, and gives the reason it works: the king sees into the case himself and has no self-interest in it, so corrupt judges cannot stand before him and the villain is too struck with the office to face out his iniquity. John Gill makes the point historically, of kings who heard causes themselves. What the eyes are is left open. John Wesley offers both readings without choosing—his very looks, or his diligent inspection into affairs—while Keil and Delitzsch, who call the phrase the seat of rectitude and set it against the seat of iniquity, take them for eyes of the mind. They note that the Greek version supplies the adjective righteous, which the Hebrew does not need.

The question about a clean heart is answered four ways. Henry hears both a challenge and a lamentation, and marks the irony that those who think themselves as good as they should be cannot say it, while those who really are good will not and dare not. He then grades the denial: we may say through grace that we are cleaner than we were, but not clean; clean from gross acts, and still not clean in heart; washed, and yet not self-washed; pure from the sins of many others, and still not from the sin that easily besets us. Keil and Delitzsch add a grammatical point to the same effect, that the possessive in from my sins is potential rather than actual—the sins meant being those one might yet fall into by not resisting temptation—and observe that self-knowledge always remains limited. Charles Ellicott concludes that satisfaction with ourselves ought never to be allowed, however far repentance has gone. Clarke alone turns the question into an answer: no man can say it, but thousands can testify that the blood of Christ has cleansed them, and he is pure who is justified freely. Gill keeps to the first half, that no part of the heart is undefiled and God alone can make it clean.

On the weights they agree, and vary only in detail. Keil and Delitzsch explain that stone and stone means stones of two sizes, so one may be deceitfully substituted for the other, the measure named standing for all. Henry makes it concrete—an under-weight for what is paid out, an over-weight for what is taken in, a scanty measure to sell by and a large one to buy by—and notes the fraud is committed under colour of doing right; God, he says, will not prosper such a trade. The child is where they genuinely part. Henry says children have not yet learned the art of dissembling and concealing their bent that grown people have, so they discover themselves early. Gill reports a contrary sense given to the word, by which the child carries himself a stranger in his doings and is not known by them, disguising himself and playing the hypocrite—and if children can do that, much more grown persons; Clarke has met the same view, that every child will dissemble. Keil and Delitzsch worry whether the word means play or work, note a proposal to emend it because it never means anything but work, and call the conjecture possible but no more. Clarke draws the practical conclusion: children give indications of the callings nature adapts them to, the future engineer visible in the little handicraftsman of two years old, and many are crossed in these early propensities to their great prejudice.
12:
The saying about the ear and the eye is treated as a bare fact with several consequences. Keil and Delitzsch refuse a rendering that would make it the ear hears and the eye sees, then say the proverb affirms a fact and that this is its plain sense—though it may be viewed from several sides, none to be rejected. The nearest is the argument from the greater: God is himself the All-hearing and All-seeing, which yields the consolation that everything seen stands under his government, and a warning they quote from the rabbis, to know what is above you—a seeing eye, a hearing ear, and all your conduct marked in his book. Matthew Henry takes it on two levels. God is the God of nature, and since hearing and seeing are the learning senses they particularly owe him acknowledgement; and he is the God of grace, for he gives the ear that hears his voice and the eye that sees his beauty, opening the understanding. John Gill supplies the contrast: a painter can paint an ear and a carver carve one, but they do not hear, and only ears that hear are of the Lord’s own make. Adam Clarke and Charles Ellicott draw the inference, that faculties so given are to be used in subserviency to his will.

On sleep the voices are careful not to condemn it. Gill calls it a great natural blessing, a gift of God which nature requires and may be loved, though not immoderately; the eye, he adds, was made for sight and not for sleep only. Clarke compares it to food—a certain measure restores nature, more oppresses and destroys life—then delivers a verdict: a lover of sleep is a paltry, insignificant character. Henry works out the discipline. Love it not for its own sake but as it fits a man for further work; allow it to the body as men allow it to their servants, because they cannot help it and will otherwise get no good of them. He explains why the loss exceeds the hours: those who love sleep contract a listless careless disposition and are still half asleep, never well awake. Keil and Delitzsch reject a proposed Arabic parallel for the verb meaning to become poor, since it means to loiter rather than to come down. Ellicott reduces the whole to four words—be up and stirring—and John Wesley to the same effect. Henry adds a modest promise: if a man does not grow rich he shall have enough, and that is as good as a feast.

The haggling buyer produces a dispute and a story. Keil and Delitzsch report a rendering with many supporters that makes the speaker a man disparaging what he owns and praising it once gone, a sentiment the ancients had proverbs of their own for. They reject it: the reflexive verb does not receive its full force so, and the word for the speaker means the possessor by acquisition, that is, the buyer. Henry, assuming the buyer, spreads the blame evenly. Men not only cheapen carelessly, as though they had no need of what they cannot go without, but run down what they know to be valuable; the seller answers by extravagantly commending his goods, so there is a fault on both sides, whereas the bargain would be made every jot as well if both spoke as they think. Henry notices the self-contradiction in the boast: a man who brags of the price he got admits he dissembled while getting it. Clarke asks whether such knavery is actionable or punishable only in another world, and tells of a mountebank who advertised that he would show every man present what was in his heart, drew an immense crowd, and kept the pledge in one sentence—that they all wished to buy cheap and sell dear—and was applauded, every hearer knowing his own heart in it.
15:
The comparison with jewels is read as a climb. Keil and Delitzsch point out that it rises by stages—there is gold, and pearls in abundance, the second always worth more than the first—so that intelligent lips stand above both, and they compare the merchant who sought goodly pearls and found one worth more than the many. Lips, as the organ of knowledge, they liken to a precious vessel. Matthew Henry gives two reasons for the preference. The first is rarity: there is gold in many a man’s pocket who has no grace in his heart, and in that age gold was plentiful and everybody wore rubies, to be bought in every town, while wisdom is rare and not purchasable of merchants at all. The second is profit, these riches being riches toward God. He notices too that appetite for the one is insatiable: most men are fond of gold, and a ruby or two will not serve, they must have a cabinet of jewels, whereas the man who has the lips of knowledge despises such things because he possesses better. Adam Clarke, Charles Ellicott, John Gill and John Wesley each say in a line that wise speech is worth more than any of them.

The proverb about the surety divides over who is being seized. Ellicott prefers take him as a pledge, meaning seize the person of the man who has gone surety, and notes that text and margin differ over the last words, read either for strangers or for a strange woman. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same rendering by elimination: the word is not a noun meaning his pledge, nor is it to be read as one ancient version has it, nor is it the intensive form, which would mean destroy him—it is the simple imperative, a form for which they can find almost no parallel. Clarke reads it differently, making the stranger the surety rather than the person stood for: if an unknown man offers himself as security, greater caution is needed, and such security taken as will prevent his running from the engagement. Henry finds two classes here, both certain to be beggars shortly and neither to be trusted—those who will be bound for anybody who asks, to oblige idle companions, and those in league with abandoned women, who have strange ways of impoverishing men to enrich themselves. Gill draws the practical rule that nothing should be lent such a man without a pledge, reports a reading making the verse a prophecy of what will become of him, stripped of everything and without a coat, and then turns it to Christ, who became surety for strangers.

On the bread of deceit the question is what the phrase denotes. Keil and Delitzsch deny that it means deceit itself, the thing a man has an appetite for, and define it as what is not gained by labour and not merited; on the gravel they offer two readings without choosing, that he will end with nothing and only evil remaining, or that the bread itself turns to gravel in his mouth. Henry keeps the sequence of sweet and bitter: the pleasure is real in the commission, the more sweet for being ill-gotten, such delight does the carnal mind take in the success of its projects; but when conscience wakes and the man sees he has been cheated, the thought is painful. Some nations, he adds, have punished malefactors by mingling gravel with their bread. Gill widens the saying to sin as such, comparing it to fruit beautiful to look at that drops into ashes when touched, and setting what sin promises—pleasure, profit, honour, liberty, peace and impunity—against what it gives, the reverse of each. Clarke keeps it narrow, to property acquired by falsehood or speculation without labour, pleasant to the slothful, but with a curse in it the issue will prove.
18:
The counsel about war draws the sharpest writing here. Adam Clarke says no precept in the book is so little regarded, since most wars are undertaken out of injustice, ambition and caprice, with no previous good counsel at all; and he traces the machinery—a minister counsels his king to war, the cabinet is brought in, and what began in caprice is maintained through necessity, with offices filled by needy dependents whose interest it is to protract the war until their debts are paid. For these ends, he says, the blood of the country is spilled and the treasure of the people exhausted; he has met with a case precisely of this kind in one French reign. Matthew Henry asks the questions in advance—whether the war should be begun, whether it is just, whether one is a match for the enemy—and once begun, by what arts it should be prosecuted, management being as necessary as courage; going to law, he notes, is a kind of going to war, and he quotes the old rule neither to urge war nor to shun it. Keil and Delitzsch report a scholar who wished to change the imperative into an infinitive, giving with management one carries on war, because a challenge to make war seemed to him contrary to the spirit of proverbial poetry; they reply that the author certainly does mean the imperative, war being disastrous unless directed with strategic skill. John Wesley reduces it to serious consideration before acting.

The talebearer is described twice. Henry pairs the vices: talebearers are commonly flatterers, insinuating themselves by fair speeches, and flatterers are commonly talebearers—so if a man fawns on you, suspect a design and stand on your guard, since he will pick out of you what makes a story elsewhere. Those who trust a man because he speaks fairly buy their own praise dearly. Charles Ellicott takes the flattery out altogether: the phrase means rather that the man is open with his lips and cannot keep them shut. Keil and Delitzsch report a rendering that turns the whole into a threefold warning against the revealer of secrets, the slanderer and the loquacious mouth, but keep the first line as a verdict carrying its own warning, to entrust nothing to a babbler. On the child who curses his parents Keil and Delitzsch distinguish carefully: the law condemned such a one to death, but the proverb does not mean that sentence, which can only seldom have been carried out, and speaks instead of the fearful end that terminates such a life. The extinguished lamp they take differently. Henry reads it of reputation, peace of mind and shortened days, the reverse of the promise attached to the commandment; Clarke reads it of posterity, the man cut off root and branch.

The last verse is textually unsettled, and both scholars say so. Gill reports that the received version follows the margin, while the written text gives an inheritance loathsome or abominable, that is, ill-gotten; he adds a derivation from an Arabic root for covetousness, and a Jewish reading that makes it an inheritance falling in without labour, which as it lightly comes lightly goes. Keil and Delitzsch canvass the same options and reject both: detested yields no sense, and avarice agrees neither with the word for inheritance nor with the phrase at the beginning, since avarice is a chronic disease. They keep the marginal reading, hastened, and link the verse to the one before—for a son of that kind the parents live too long, and he takes the property by violence before it is due. Henry says such an estate is soon ripe and soon rotten; Clarke calls speculation in trade a public nuisance and curse, leading to idleness, pride and fraud; and Ellicott finds the pattern in a patriarch punished for the selfishness by which he gained a birthright and the fraud by which he took a blessing.
22:
On the refusal of revenge the voices converge, and all notice the same thing about the promise. Keil and Delitzsch put it exactly: the verse does not tell a man to leave the taking of vengeance to God, and the promise is not that God will avenge him but that God will help him. What is required is that, renouncing dependence on himself, he commit deliverance and vindication into other hands. The law of love, they add, asks not merely that a man keep the rule of requital but surpass it. Matthew Henry makes the same distinction and takes comfort in it: God does not say he will punish the man who injured you, but that he will save you, and that is enough; he will protect you, so that passing by one injury shall not, as is commonly feared, expose you to another. Henry presses the interior side too, that revenge must not be entertained even in the heart—do not please yourself with the thought that you will one day be quits—and supplies a test: never say you will do what you cannot in faith pray God to assist you in. Charles Ellicott agrees that what to look for is deliverance from an enemy’s attacks rather than vengeance on him, since he is to be forgiven; Adam Clarke goes further and says to pray meanwhile for the enemy’s conversion; and John Gill states the ground, that vengeance belongs elsewhere.

The proverb about the weights has been given once already, and the repetition is itself explained. Henry offers two reasons: it is a sin doubly hated, as lying is named twice in another list of what God hates, and it was probably much practised and so made light of, under the pretence that since everybody used false weights there was no trading without them. He takes the added clause, that a false balance is not good, as saying more than the first—the practice is not only abominable to God but unprofitable to the man himself, a bargain made by fraud proving a losing bargain in the end. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by grammar, treating the phrase as a neuter understatement: not good, that is, bad and pernicious, for the deceiver succeeds only in appearance and in reality fails. Gill too supposes the sin was common among those addressed.

The last saying raises the hardest question, and Keil and Delitzsch answer it carefully. The first line is borrowed from a psalm, but there it means the gracious assistance by which a man takes his steps, whereas here it states the general truth that man proposes and God disposes. They then mark what is left to the man: he is free to turn this way or that and decide on one course or another, and is responsible for it; but the conditions co-operating in every step are not of his contriving, and the consequences lie beyond his power, each step being a link in a chain. Henry draws the inference. All our natural actions depend on providence and our spiritual actions on grace; the best man is no better than God makes him, and the goings even of a strong man—which, he says, is what the word signifies—are of the Lord, strength without God being weakness. Since we understand our own way so little that we do not know what is good for ourselves, we may as well make a virtue of necessity and commit it to the one who holds it. Clarke condenses it into a saying he quotes from an old writer, that they who will carve for themselves shall cut their fingers. Ellicott turns it into prayer: the less a man sees of his own road the more reason to ask to be shown it. Gill takes the steps on three levels—the literal power of motion, the business of civil life, and the going of faith.
25:
The first of these sayings is read two incompatible ways. Keil and Delitzsch reject the received sense outright. They dismiss the construction that makes a man’s snare devour the holy, since the phrase expresses something suffered rather than done, and call the old versions giving calumniating or devoting arbitrary. Their reading takes the verb as speaking rashly and the noun as the exclamation a man utters when he declares a thing dedicated—so the snare is to cry holy in haste and look into the vow only afterwards. Charles Ellicott arrives at the same: it gets a man into trouble to say thoughtlessly that something is dedicated, and then, having vowed, to ask whether he can keep his word. Matthew Henry keeps the sense of sacrilege, of holy things converted to private use, and extends it in a direction of his own—those who hurry over their praying and preaching and huddle them up out of impatience to be done may be said to devour what is holy. On the second clause he agrees that it is a snare to ask after the fact how a vow may be evaded, and notes that if the words were ambiguous the fault lay in making them so. Adam Clarke reads the first half as sacrilege too, and the second as a warning that fitness should be weighed before the vow, not after; he then reports, with visible discomfort, that his old English Bible renders the verse as though it were about vowing to saints, and asks whether the translator can really have written it so. John Gill states the plain case of tithes turned to private use.

On the wise king the figure is agreed and its limits marked. Keil and Delitzsch identify the wheel as the threshing-cart’s, to be understood with the winnowing fork, and warn expressly against thinking of the punishment of the wheel, which occurs only as a terrible custom of war; most older interpreters, they add, took the word metaphorically, as manner or way, or as the wheel of fortune, and so as misfortune. Clarke describes the machinery—grain was separated by oxen trampling the sheaves or by a rough-shod wheel driven over them—and makes the same exclusion in his own words, that Asiatic kings often threshed their people to bring out their property, but that this is not meant here. Ellicott and Gill prefer winnows to scatters, Gill adding that the king breaks their confederacies. Henry turns the image into administration: bringing the wheel over them means putting the laws in execution and quashing their projects, and it requires a magistrate both pious and prudent. John Wesley says he punishes them as their offences deserve.

The candle of the Lord is defined narrowly by the scholars and qualified by one preacher. Keil and Delitzsch point out that the language has a separate word for the self-conscious personal spirit as distinct from the spirit of a beast, and that it is used here, naming the life breathed immediately into the body; what the proverb says could not be said of an animal, since what is figuratively represented is the mystery of self-consciousness. The commoner word, they note, is deliberately avoided, denoting not the power of self-consciousness but the medium of bodily life. Henry calls conscience God’s deputy in the soul, a candle not only lighted by him but for him, and divides its work—by reason we know other men and dive into their designs, by conscience we know ourselves, the faculty praising what is good and condemning what is otherwise. Ellicott and Wesley add that the searching reaches the inmost thoughts, the word for the body standing here for the heart. Gill alone insists on how dim the candle now is: bright and burning at first, through sin it has become feeble, so that men grope by it and it is candle light at best beside the greater light of revelation.
28:
The pair of words that guard the king proves untranslatable. Keil and Delitzsch say no couple of words in their own language covers them: of God they render grace and truth, of men love and truth, of the two-sided divine forces kindness and truth. They then set the verse against a better-known formula. Elsewhere a throne is supported with judgment and justice, but here government must have love at its centre—the king acts on the line of right, and within that circle love is the determining motive. Matthew Henry notices that mercy is named twice and takes the hint, calling mercy and truth the glories of God’s throne. Charles Ellicott explains the mechanism: the love a king shows his subjects draws the same out of them, and that keeps his throne safe—as mercy shown from above inspires reverent fear, where harshness would have made a slave or driven a man into rebellion. Adam Clarke calls these the brightest jewels in the crown, and John Gill notes the words may be rendered grace and truth and so applied to Christ.

The saying about young and old draws a shrewd observation and a rebuke. Clarke notices that each age has its own vanity: scarcely any young man affects to be wise or learned, but all delight to show their strength and be reputed strong, and agility they particularly affect; old men, having given up strength, affect wisdom instead, and are fond of being reputed wise. Henry treats it as a rule of mutual respect, neither age despising the other—the young are fit for action and break through difficulties the aged cannot grapple with, the old are fit for counsel—and quotes the tag that labour belongs to the young and honour to the aged. He guards the first half with the condition that the strength be used well and neither be proud of it nor trust to it, and Gill says the same. Ellicott turns the second half into a warning to the old: if they do not receive the honour due them the fault is their own, for not having spent their earlier years so as to make old age venerable. Keil and Delitzsch keep to etymology, deriving the word for the old man from the hanging chin.

The last verse is disputed in text and sense, and Clarke widens the question to the whole chapter, noting that six verses are missing from two ancient versions while four stand in a different place, and confessing he cannot account for it unless leaves were misplaced in the manuscripts. On the wound itself he stands alone. Taking the word from a root meaning to join together, he asks whether it refers to the scar formed when the two lips of a wound are brought together in healing, the discharge having purged away the lacerated ends of fibres and vessels—so that stripes, though they hurt, discharge the moral evil of the soul. Keil and Delitzsch cannot settle the predicate: the marginal reading gives a noun found elsewhere only of the purification of women, which they call syntactically hard and scarcely original, while a rendering making deep wounds find their cure by means that bring suffering would need a different pronoun, and is besides constrained. Ellicott renders it plainly as wounds which cut into the flesh and blows felt in the inmost recesses of the heart, and states the harsh conclusion: kindness is thrown away upon some people, who can only be touched by punishment. Henry says the same in three steps—many need severe rebukes; they sometimes do great good, as corrosives eat out the proud flesh of a wound; and those who most need them can worst bear them. John Wesley notes that the stripes reach the inward man by subduing vile affections, and Gill turns the figure round at the last, to the blue wounds and stripes that heal.
